stories.headline: Wall Street ends August down on Monday: S&P 7,686, Dow −374 as oil jump hits stocks
stories.dek: Indexes still posted monthly gains. The 10-year yield rose to 4.75% after the Iran flare-up.
stories.caveman: Monday closed the month in the red. The S&P 500 fell 25.62 points, or 0.33%, to 7,686.14. The Dow lost 374.09 points, or 0.7%, to 53,185.90. The Nasdaq slipped 0.12% to 26,370.89. Oil jumped after U.S. and Iranian forces traded fire over the weekend, and that scared inflation watchers. Still, August was a win on paper: the S&P rose about 2.6% for the month, the Nasdaq about 3.9%, and the Dow logged its fifth straight green month. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed to 4.75%, near levels seen when the White House talked about intervening in the bond market two weeks ago. Traders go into September watching jobs on Friday and the Fed on Sept. 15–16.
stories.why_it_matters: Taipei opens into a U.S. month-end fade plus a Middle East oil spike. Chip and export names feel both.
stories.camps: Bulls point to August gains and AI demand. Hawks say oil plus Fed hike odds mean tighter money. Workers and renters feel the yield, not the monthly chart.

terms.explain: A basket of 500 big U.S. companies. Many people treat it as ‘the market.’
The index finished August higher than July even if the last day fell.
The interest rate on a 10-year U.S. government bond. When it rises, mortgages and loans often get pricier.
A fast rise in oil prices. It can push gasoline and inflation fears higher.

stories.image_alt: Wall Street trading scene used in AP market wrap

stories.headline: Oil settles Monday: WTI $85.76, Brent $90.49 after Hormuz clash; only ~5 ships a day
stories.dek: Both contracts rose about 2.8%. August still finished with small monthly gains.
stories.caveman: Crude closed higher on the first U.S.-Iran firefight in a month. West Texas Intermediate for October settled at $85.76 a barrel, up $2.36 or 2.83%. Brent for November settled at $90.49, up $2.39 or 2.71%. For August, WTI was up about 1.3% and Brent about 0.4%. Shipping data said only about five commodity vessels a day crossed the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend — far below the roughly 100-a-day pace before the war. A tanker was reported hit by a projectile on an inbound run. The market is pricing transit risk, not a sudden loss of wells. Pump prices and Asian import bills feel that premium first.
stories.why_it_matters: Taiwan imports almost all its oil. A Hormuz scare raises freight, insurance, and gasoline costs even if no barrels vanish overnight.
stories.camps: Energy traders say war risk is back in the price. Doves say tit-for-tat military hits often fade without a supply cut. Ship crews and consumers pay the insurance first.

terms.explain: The main U.S. oil price. Quoted in dollars per barrel.
The main global oil price. Many Asian cargoes track it.
A narrow waterway by Iran and Oman. About a fifth of world oil used to pass here.
Extra dollars baked into the oil price because traders fear a fight will block ships.

stories.image_alt: Oil pump jacks in a field

stories.headline: FedWatch: 66% chance of a September quarter-point hike after Warsh and oil spike
stories.dek: Mortgage rates already near 7%. Jobs print Sept. 4; CPI Sept. 11; FOMC Sept. 15–16.
stories.caveman: Rate-hike bets climbed again on Monday. CME FedWatch put about a 66% chance the Fed raises by a quarter point at the Sept. 15–16 meeting, and roughly 50% odds of another hike by December. That is hotter than the mid-to-high 50s traders priced after Warsh’s Jackson Hole talk. Chair Kevin Warsh said inflation has not ‘meaningfully improved’ and the Fed has ‘work to do.’ Hawks say sticky prices need action. Doves say hiking into an oil supply shock is a mistake. Mortgage rates already hover near 7%. The next big clues: August jobs on Sept. 4 and CPI on Sept. 11.
stories.why_it_matters: A U.S. hike can lift the dollar and squeeze global growth stocks — including Asian tech that Taipei watches every morning.
stories.camps: Hawks want a hike to prove the 2% target is real. Doves say oil from war is not the same as overheating demand. Homebuyers feel 7% mortgages either way.

terms.explain: A tool that turns futures prices into odds the Fed will hike, hold, or cut.
Raising the policy rate by 0.25 percentage points. A common small step.
A monthly U.S. inflation report based on a basket of goods and services.
The committee that sets U.S. short-term interest rates.
What banks charge to borrow for a house. Near 7% makes buying harder.

stories.image_alt: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh at Jackson Hole
stories.image_credit: Photo: Natalie Behring / Getty Images via Marketplace

stories.headline: Dollar slips 0.28% as yuan hits a 3.5-year high; Bessent warns against hiking on oil shocks
stories.dek: China’s August manufacturing PMI rose to 49.8. Markets hear a Treasury–Fed split.
stories.caveman: The dollar took a step back on Monday. The U.S. Dollar Index fell about 0.28% while the Chinese yuan climbed to a roughly 3.5-year high. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Fed traditionally does not raise rates just because of a supply shock — a soft jab after Chair Warsh sounded hawkish and oil jumped. China’s August manufacturing PMI came in at 49.8, a bit better than feared but still under 50, which means slight contraction. Non-manufacturing PMI was stuck at 49.0. Higher oil and higher hike odds limited how far the dollar fell. FX desks are watching who wins the story: inflation fight or oil-from-war exception.
stories.why_it_matters: A softer dollar can ease pressure on Asian exporters and on Taiwan’s FX desk, but a Fed–Treasury quarrel adds noise.
stories.camps: Treasury wants patience on supply-driven oil spikes. Fed hawks want rates up if inflation stays sticky. Exporters like a weaker dollar; importers fear oil.

terms.explain: A score of the U.S. dollar versus a basket of other big currencies.
China’s currency. A stronger yuan makes Chinese goods a bit pricier abroad.
A survey of factories. Above 50 usually means growth; below 50 means shrinkage.
When prices jump because stuff is scarce or blocked, not because shoppers suddenly spend more.

stories.image_alt: Currency and markets illustration

stories.headline: Apple files ‘shocking’ MacBook forensics: ex-engineer used Apple schematic at OpenAI
stories.dek: Filing says Chang Liu trained an AI agent on LTspice and told a colleague to destroy evidence. Hearing Oct. 1.
stories.caveman: Apple turned up the heat on Monday. In its trade-secrets suit against OpenAI and former Apple engineers Chang Liu and Tang Tan, Apple told the court that forensics on Liu’s returned MacBook show he downloaded a confidential Apple circuit schematic in March — two months after leaving — and used it for power-conversion work at OpenAI. Messages describe him training an AI agent to run LTspice simulations. Apple also says Liu told a colleague to destroy evidence after learning of Apple’s probe, and that the colleague agreed. OpenAI calls the suit meritless and says it does not want Apple secrets. Judge Edward Davila hears arguments on Oct. 1.
stories.why_it_matters: Big AI labs hire from Apple and chip makers. Who owns the schematics can shape Taiwan-linked supply chains and future gadgets.
stories.camps: Apple says secrets walked out the door and are still in use. OpenAI says the case is aggressive and personal. Engineers caught in the middle just want clear rules.

terms.explain: Private company recipes and designs that rivals are not supposed to take.
A careful dig through a computer’s files and logs to see what was copied or deleted.
Software engineers use to test electronic circuits on a computer before building them.
Asking a judge to force early sharing of documents and devices, before normal slow timelines.

stories.image_alt: Apple and OpenAI lawsuit coverage image

stories.headline: Nvidia puts $3.5B into MediaTek bonds as custom AI chips threaten its moat
stories.dek: Part of MediaTek’s record $3.9B overseas convertible deal; Alphabet joined too. MediaTek adopts NVLink Fusion.
stories.caveman: Nvidia is writing a huge check to keep custom AI chips inside its racks. On Monday it said it will buy $3.5 billion of MediaTek convertible bonds — the bulk of MediaTek’s record $3.9 billion overseas convertible-bond raise. Alphabet also bought some of the same bonds; the size was not disclosed. The bonds were priced Aug. 31 and are expected to close around Sept. 8. Conversion price was reported near NT$4,513.75, about a 15% premium over MediaTek’s NT$3,925 close that day — not a 115% premium. In return, MediaTek will adopt Nvidia’s NVLink Fusion so customer-built custom XPUs can plug into Nvidia rack-scale systems. The deal also covers RTX/DGX Spark PCs and Dimensity Auto chips. The U.S. angle: Nvidia is defending its interconnect moat while hyperscalers design their own accelerators. Fans say custom silicon is coming anyway, so Nvidia wants the wires. Critics of Nvidia’s ‘circular’ financing — including Bernstein’s Stacy Rasgon and short-seller Michael Burry — worry the chipmaker funds partners who then buy more Nvidia gear. The pattern follows Nvidia’s recent up-to-$105 billion OpenAI Ohio guarantee.
stories.why_it_matters: If custom chips still need Nvidia’s rack fabric, Nvidia keeps the toll booth even when customers design their own silicon.
stories.camps: Nvidia and bulls say interconnects and full systems still win. Critics say circular money muddies real demand. MediaTek gets capital; Taiwan already told the ECB story from its side.

terms.explain: Debt that can turn into company stock later. Investors get a bond first, shares if the price works.
Nvidia’s high-speed link that lets chips talk inside a big AI rack. Fusion lets non-Nvidia chips join that fabric.
A custom AI chip a cloud or lab designs for itself, not a standard Nvidia GPU.
When a seller funds customers or partners who then spend on the seller’s products. Critics say it can inflate demand.
How much higher the stock-conversion price sits above today’s share price. Here ~15% over the Aug. 31 close.

stories.image_alt: Nvidia and MediaTek AI partnership imagery from Yahoo Finance / Quartz coverage
stories.image_credit: Photo: Ying Tang/NurPhoto via Getty Images / Quartz via Yahoo Finance

stories.headline: John Ternus becomes Apple CEO today; Cook shifts to executive chairman
stories.dek: First CEO change in 15 years. His first big stage: the Sept. 9 ‘Surprise and shine’ event.
stories.caveman: Tuesday is handoff day in Cupertino. John Ternus, Apple’s longtime hardware engineering chief and a 25-year company veteran, becomes CEO on Sept. 1, 2026 — the date Apple set when it announced the plan in April. Tim Cook, CEO since 2011, becomes executive chairman. The board said the plan was unanimous and long prepared. Ternus inherits an AI race, a pricey stock, and a product calendar that includes new iPhones eight days later on Sept. 9. Analysts expect more hardware bets and maybe bigger deals than Cook preferred. Workers and suppliers will watch whether Apple stays a logistics machine or swings harder into new gadgets. Markets usually shrug at planned tech successions — until the first product flop or hit.
stories.why_it_matters: Apple is a top customer for Taiwan’s chip and assembly chain. A new CEO can shift order books and R&D priorities.
stories.camps: Bulls like an engineer-CEO for AI hardware. Skeptics say Cook’s supply-chain magic is hard to replace. Factory workers care about volumes, not the title on the badge.

terms.explain: Cook keeps a top board job and influence but is no longer day-to-day CEO.
A planned change of company leader. Apple announced this one in April for a Sept. 1 start.
The teams that design phones, Macs, and chips inside the case.
Apple’s big fall product show. Ternus’s first major stage as CEO is eight days after he starts.

stories.image_alt: Tim Cook and John Ternus at Apple Park

stories.headline: Apple’s Sept. 9 ‘Surprise and shine’ event tees up iPhone 18 Pro and rumored foldable
stories.dek: Invites went out Aug. 26. First Ternus-era keynote; Siri AI and Watch updates also expected.
stories.caveman: The invite is out and the clock is loud. Apple set its fall event for Wednesday, Sept. 9 at 10 a.m. Pacific in Cupertino, tagged ‘Surprise and shine.’ It will be the first big iPhone keynote under new CEO John Ternus. Analysts expect iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, with a rumored book-style foldable often called iPhone Ultra. Regular iPhone 18 models may wait until spring 2027. Also on the rumor board: Apple Watch Series 12, Ultra 4, and a rebuilt Siri AI. Memory shortages could lift prices. None of this is confirmed until the stage lights go on. Pre-orders often follow within days.
stories.why_it_matters: iPhone cycles drive Taiwan component makers. A foldable would open new display and hinge orders — or flop and idle lines.
stories.camps: Fans want a real new form factor. Skeptics say foldables are pricey niche toys. Supply-chain workers need firm unit forecasts, not slogans.

terms.explain: Apple’s big streamed product show. New phones usually appear here.
A phone that opens like a book into a larger screen. Still unconfirmed by Apple.
Apple’s rebuilt voice assistant using modern large-language-model tech.
The days you can reserve a new phone before it ships to stores.

stories.image_alt: Apple September event invitation graphic

stories.headline: Trump vows to ‘hit them hard,’ posts AI video of Kharg ‘smithereens’; no strike happened
stories.dek: U.S. hit Larak launchers; Iran fired on two Jordan bases. Iranian media say three died at Larak.
stories.caveman: The six-month U.S.-Iran war flared again. U.S. Central Command said forces struck two Iranian missile launchers on Larak Island after Guards units were seen readying rockets with sea mines for the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian media said three people were killed. Tehran said it then fired on two U.S. air bases in Jordan. President Trump told Fox, ‘We’re going to hit them hard,’ and posted AI-made videos claiming Iran’s Kharg oil terminal was ‘blown to smithereens.’ A U.S. official said Kharg was not hit. Iran’s oil chief called the post laughable. Trump also said there was ‘no reason’ for nuclear weapons because Iran was already ‘totally defeated militarily.’ Pezeshkian still said continuing the war helps no one.
stories.why_it_matters: Kharg handles most of Iran’s oil exports. Even fake attack videos can jolt oil, shipping, and Asian fuel costs.
stories.camps: White House frames limited self-defense and economic pressure. Tehran calls U.S. strikes aggression and mocks AI threats. Gulf neighbors and ship crews sit in the blast radius of both.

terms.explain: A small Iranian island by the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. said it hit launchers there Sunday.
Iran’s main oil export hub. It handled about 90% of Iran’s oil exports before the war.
A computer-made video that looks real. Trump posted one of an attack that did not occur.
U.S. penalties that hit foreign banks or firms for dealing with Iran.

stories.image_alt: Coverage image related to Trump Kharg Island posts

stories.headline: Zelensky locks visit dates with Witkoff and Kushner; says intel shows Putin still wants war
stories.dek: Envoys have yet to visit Kyiv. Bessent met Russia’s Siluanov at G20; Kyiv says it was not told.
stories.caveman: Ukraine’s president pushed the calendar on Monday. Volodymyr Zelensky said he held a ‘detailed and constructive’ call with Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to lock dates for their first visit to Ukraine. The pair have gone to Moscow more than once but still have not been to Kyiv. Zelensky said September ‘can change a lot,’ briefed them on a front where Russian gains are ‘sparse’ and costly, and separately warned that Ukrainian and allied intel say Vladimir Putin still wants to keep fighting. In North Carolina, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov at a G20 gathering — Moscow’s first such appearance in years. A Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent Kyiv knew nothing about that meeting.
stories.why_it_matters: Peace-talk choreography shapes Europe’s security and energy risk that Asia prices every week.
stories.camps: Kyiv wants envoys on Ukrainian soil and a plan that is not surrender. Moscow signals it can wait. U.S. envoys sell a Trump peace track while Ukraine’s public is left out of some side meetings.

terms.explain: A person sent by a president to talk peace or pressure without being the ambassador.
A club of big economies. Finance ministers met in North Carolina this week.
An early U.S. outline to end the Russia-Ukraine war. Later trimmed; Moscow rejected revisions.
What spy and military agencies conclude about an enemy’s real goals.

stories.image_alt: President Zelensky in his office

stories.headline: France takes UN Security Council presidency Sept. 1; plans Ukraine meeting in high-level week
stories.dek: Macron expected at the General Assembly. Paris also wants a Middle East/Palestine stock-take.
stories.caveman: New York’s big table changes hosts today. France assumes the UN Security Council presidency for September — its 70th turn in the chair. A diplomatic source told Ukrinform Paris will convene a separate Council meeting on Ukraine, likely during UN General Assembly high-level week, possibly with ministers or even Zelensky. French President Emmanuel Macron is expected in New York. Paris also wants attention on the Middle East, including a look at the year since the New York Declaration on Palestine and the two-state track. A Council presidency cannot force peace alone. It can set the agenda, draft statements, and force public arguments when veto powers disagree.
stories.why_it_matters: UN week sets talking points that move markets and aid budgets from New York to Taipei desks watching Europe and the Gulf.
stories.camps: France wants Ukraine and Palestine on the stage. Russia and allies may push back on wording. Smaller states want airtime that veto powers often crowd out.

terms.explain: A one-month rotating job that runs meeting schedules and helps draft texts.
Late September days when presidents and ministers flood New York for speeches.
The idea of Israel and a Palestinian state living side by side.
Any of the five permanent Council members can block a binding resolution.

stories.image_alt: UN-related photo from Ukrinform coverage

stories.headline: Board of Peace envoy Mladenov: Gaza ceasefire risks collapse without roadmap buy-in
stories.dek: Hamas says it approved the next-phase plan; Netanyahu has publicly rejected key parts.
stories.caveman: The ceasefire is holding on paper and fraying in practice. Nickolay Mladenov, high representative for Trump’s Board of Peace, told Al Jazeera the failure of both sides to follow the next-phase roadmap ‘threatens a collapse of the ceasefire in Gaza,’ and that a return to war would be devastating. Hamas says it approved the roadmap and wants Israel held to it. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has publicly rejected parts of the plan, including aspects of an international force and sequencing of withdrawal versus Hamas disarmament. Morocco agreed to join a stabilization force; Israel vetoed Türkiye’s role. Kushner’s earlier shuttle did not break the deadlock. Civilians still die under a ceasefire that does not feel like peace.
stories.why_it_matters: A Gaza collapse would spike oil risk, refugee pressure, and global protest politics that reach Taiwan campuses and markets.
stories.camps: Board of Peace says this roadmap is the only path. Netanyahu insists full Hamas disarmament first. Gazan families want safety and aid, not another sequencing fight.

terms.explain: A U.S.-backed body tasked with advancing Trump’s Gaza plan after the Oct. 2025 ceasefire.
A step-by-step deal for disarmament, governance, and troop moves after a ceasefire.
Proposed foreign troops to help keep order while Gaza transitions.
The fight over whether Israel withdraws before Hamas disarms, or the reverse.

stories.image_alt: Gaza ceasefire diplomacy coverage

stories.headline: IndieBound: Yesteryear still No. 1 hardcover fiction; Calamity Club No. 2, Whistler No. 3
stories.dek: Week ending Aug. 26 chart. Indie shops keep literary and satirical debuts ahead of romantasy.
stories.caveman: At independent bookstores, the top shelf still looks literary. For the week ending Aug. 26, IndieBound’s national hardcover fiction list kept Caro Claire Burke’s Yesteryear at No. 1 for a 20th week. Kathryn Stockett’s The Calamity Club rose to No. 2. Ann Patchett’s Whistler sat at No. 3. Sheila Masterson’s The Poison Daughter arrived new at No. 6 on the indie list even as it leads some mass charts. Indie buyers are rewarding satire about tradwife fame, Depression-era sisterhood, and Patchett’s quiet novel about connection. Chain and online lists can look louder. Indies still set the ‘who’s hot in literary fiction’ mood for U.S. readers.
stories.why_it_matters: U.S. literary trends travel through translation rights and English-language shelves that Taipei readers browse too.
stories.camps: Indie booksellers push literary fiction and debuts. Algorithm charts push romantasy and thrillers. Midlist authors without TikTok buzz get squeezed either way.

terms.explain: A bestseller list from U.S. independent bookstores, often different from Amazon or big chains.
New novels sold in hard covers — usually the first pricey edition.
Online stars who sell a hyper-traditional homemaker image. Yesteryear satirizes that world.
Novels prized for style and ideas more than pure plot thrills.

stories.image_alt: Cover of Yesteryear by Caro Claire Burke

stories.headline: Theo of Golden holds Publishers Weekly overall No. 1 with 49,942 print copies; 1.55M YTD
stories.dek: Allen Levi’s quiet paperback keeps beating louder debuts on the Aug. 31 Circana week.
stories.caveman: The sleeper will not sleep. On Publishers Weekly’s top overall list for the week of Aug. 31, Allen Levi’s Theo of Golden stayed at No. 1 with 49,942 print copies sold that week and about 1.55 million year-to-date. The Atria paperback has 39 weeks on the list. It beat brand-new noise like Pardon My Book at No. 2 and Freida McFadden’s Brain Damage at No. 3. Booksellers call it a word-of-mouth kindness novel — creative generosity, wonder, soft ties between strangers. In a year of podcast dumps and romantasy spikes, a quiet book still can own the cash register.
stories.why_it_matters: When a paperback stays No. 1 for months, it shapes U.S. reading taste and what foreign scouts buy next.
stories.camps: Indie and chain fans treat Theo as comfort literary. Publishers chase the next viral debut. Authors without a long build rarely get 39 weeks.

terms.explain: The sales tracker Publishers Weekly uses for many U.S. print bestseller lists.
Copies sold since Jan. 1 this year. Theo is over 1.5 million.
Sales driven by friends telling friends, not only ads or influencers.
A cheaper soft cover. Theo’s big run is in this format.

stories.image_alt: Cover of Theo of Golden by Allen Levi

stories.headline: Freida McFadden’s Brain Damage debuts No. 3 overall on PW Top 100
stories.dek: 32,775 Circana print copies for the week ended Aug. 22 (Aug. 31 PW). Cheap thriller paperbacks keep surging.
stories.caveman: Who’s hot in U.S. print: Freida McFadden again. Brain Damage — a psychological thriller from Poisoned Pen Press — debuted at No. 3 on Publishers Weekly’s overall Top 100 with 32,775 Circana BookScan print copies for the week ended Aug. 22, as reported in the Aug. 31 PW list. That sits just under Pardon My Book’s 49,297 at No. 2 (context only; Monday already led with that nonfiction hit) and ahead of The Poison Daughter’s 27,068 at No. 4 overall / No. 1 hardcover fiction — do not treat Poison Daughter as this card’s lead; Monday already did. The signal is the McFadden-style paperback thriller surge: fast, cheap, TikTok-friendly hits that still move tens of thousands of paper copies in a single week.
stories.why_it_matters: U.S. ‘who’s hot’ charts set what bookstores reorder and what foreign houses buy next.
stories.camps: Thriller fans want twisty, fast paperbacks. Literary hardcovers fight for shelf space. Retailers chase whatever BookScan says moved last week.

terms.explain: The main U.S. tracker of print books sold through many stores. PW uses it for bestseller lists.
Publishers Weekly’s combined ranking of the week’s best-selling print books across formats.
A softcover novel sold in bookstores. Often cheaper and faster-moving than hardcovers.
The imprint that published Brain Damage. Part of the Sourcebooks family.

stories.image_alt: Cover of Brain Damage by Freida McFadden
stories.image_credit: Photo: Publishers Weekly / Poisoned Pen Press cover

stories.headline: IndieBound nonfiction: Regime Change No. 1; The Nerd Reich debuts at No. 4
stories.dek: Haberman and Swan’s Trump second-term book leads. Gil Durán’s tech-authoritarian critique arrives.
stories.caveman: Political nonfiction owns the indie front table. For the week ending Aug. 26, IndieBound’s hardcover nonfiction list had Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan’s Regime Change: Inside the Imperial Presidency of Donald Trump at No. 1 for a ninth week. New at No. 4: Gil Durán’s The Nerd Reich, a starred-review takedown of tech-billionaire politics around Trump’s circle. David Sedaris essays held No. 2. The split is clear: readers want inside-the-White-House reporting and a sharper critique of Silicon Valley power. Barstool sports memoirs may win some mass charts; indie shops are stacking Haberman, Swan, and Durán.
stories.why_it_matters: These books set the U.S. argument about Trump, tech, and democracy that English-language media worldwide echo.
stories.camps: Trump critics treat Regime Change as evidence. Supporters call it hostile press. Tech workers split between Durán’s alarm and ‘innovation needs freedom’ pushback.

terms.explain: A 2026 nonfiction book on Trump’s second term by two New York Times reporters.
Gil Durán’s book arguing some tech billionaires push anti-democratic politics.
Fact books in hard covers — memoirs, history, politics.
A rare strong tip from trade magazines that a book is especially good.

stories.image_alt: Cover of Regime Change by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan

stories.headline: Israeli forces seize UNRWA’s Kalandia Training Centre; 340 refugee students at risk
stories.dek: Aug. 25 entry in East Jerusalem. UN Secretary-General condemns unlawful presence on UN premises.
stories.caveman: A UN school building became a flashpoint. On Aug. 25, Israeli forces forcibly entered UNRWA’s Kalandia Training Centre in occupied East Jerusalem. Israeli officials then indicated the premises had been seized. It was the fifth unauthorized entry since May. The centre, open since 1952, trains Palestine refugee youth in job skills. The UN Secretary-General and the UN Special Coordinator condemned the move, warning it immediately threatens education for 340 students and thousands more in coming years. Clashes nearby left at least nine injured that day. UN premises are supposed to be inviolable under international law. Aid groups say the seizure is another shock to an already squeezed West Bank response.
stories.why_it_matters: Attacks on UN schools shrink the last public services for refugees — a humanitarian red line watched worldwide.
stories.camps: UN and UNRWA call the seizure illegal. Israeli authorities claim security and property grounds. Students and parents lose classrooms either way.

terms.explain: The UN agency that runs schools, clinics, and aid for Palestine refugees.
UNRWA’s oldest vocational school in East Jerusalem, founded in 1952.
The rule that UN buildings should not be entered or taken by a host military.
The eastern part of Jerusalem occupied by Israel in 1967; status is disputed under international law.

stories.image_alt: Palestinian residents affected by settler takeover in East Jerusalem, from OCHA report

stories.headline: Gaza Flash Appeal only ~40% funded; kitchens still cook 712,000 meals a day
stories.dek: UN briefed Security Council Aug. 26. Shelter stocks thin before winter rain; two-thirds of Gaza hard to reach.
stories.caveman: Aid math is ugly. At an Aug. 26 Security Council briefing, the UN’s interim Special Coordinator said the 2026 Flash Appeal for Palestinians was only about 40% funded while needs stay immense. In Gaza, partners were still preparing about 712,000 meals a day through 95 kitchens as of Aug. 20, and had reached about 172,000 households with food parcels by Aug. 23. Around two-thirds of Gaza remains inaccessible or heavily restricted. Shelter and non-food stocks for the rainy season are depleted. Electricity is scarce. The ceasefire framework has not stopped airstrikes near warehouses or the squeeze on families. Funding gaps turn into empty shelves.
stories.why_it_matters: Underfunded appeals mean more hunger and disease — and more regional instability priced into energy and shipping.
stories.camps: UN agencies beg for cash and access. Donors cite fatigue and politics. Gazan civilians need food and tents, not another funding percentage slide.

terms.explain: A UN ask for billions to fund food, water, shelter, and health for people in crisis.
How much of the asked money has actually arrived. About 40% means most needs are unpaid.
Cooked meals from aid kitchens, not just dry bags of flour.
A military boundary in Gaza that limits where civilians and aid can go.

stories.headline: Nepal flash floods: OCHA says 903 dead, 4,200+ missing as of Monday morning
stories.dek: 267 injured confirmed. Kathmandu Post: >10,000 rescued; ~590 foreign nationals still missing.
stories.caveman: People, not spectacle: Nepal is still counting the missing after last week’s Himalayan flash floods. On Aug. 31 the UN’s OCHA said authorities had confirmed 903 dead and 267 injured as of that morning, with more than 4,200 people still missing. The Kathmandu Post the same day reported 903 bodies recovered, about 4,200 unaccounted for, and more than 10,000 people rescued — including 323 foreign nationals — while about 590 foreigners from dozens of countries remained missing. Aid is scaling: India and China sent tunnel-rescue and forensic teams; Singapore prepared disaster-victim ID help; Australia raised humanitarian support. Locals are returning to villages buried in mud that no longer look like home. Government officials say they are now asking foreign partners for specialized gear; critics ask why early warning and preparedness were thin before the rivers rose. Identifying bodies is slow; families wait on lists taped to walls.
stories.why_it_matters: A climate-linked mountain disaster is also a cross-border missing-persons crisis for tourists and migrant workers.
stories.camps: Officials stress international rescue and DNA ID help. Critics question preparedness and early warning. Survivors need shelter, clean water, and names for the missing — not viral wreckage clips.

terms.explain: The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs. It tracks disasters and organizes aid.
A fast, violent flood — often from glacier or river collapse — that hits before people can flee.
People not confirmed dead or alive. Families wait while search and DNA ID continue.
Specialist work — often DNA — to name recovered bodies so families can grieve and claim remains.
A shared base where aid groups plan and share info. OCHA said partners were setting one up in Nuwakot.

stories.headline: Kyiv under fifth day of jet-drone blitz; overnight blasts injure 4 including 2 children
stories.dek: Ballistic missiles hit after Aug. 31 drone waves. Earlier barrage in the capital region killed dozens.
stories.caveman: Ukraine’s capital cannot catch its breath. Into Sept. 1, Russia kept pounding Kyiv after a fifth straight day of jet-powered drone attacks on Aug. 31. Overnight, dozens of explosions rocked the city within minutes; authorities said four people were injured in Solomyanskyi district, including two children. Earlier Monday, regional officials reported more blast injuries around Kyiv as warehouses and homes burned. Ukraine said it intercepted most of a large drone wave overnight into Aug. 31. The multi-day blitz has already killed dozens in the capital region, including children on earlier days. Air-raid life — shelters, closed shops, sleepless nights — is the civilian story behind the diplomacy talks.
stories.why_it_matters: Civilian bombing undercuts peace talks and keeps European energy and security risk high for Asian markets.
stories.camps: Kyiv calls it terror against cities. Moscow claims military aims. Families in apartment blocks just want the sirens to stop.

terms.explain: A faster drone with a small jet engine. Harder for air defenses than slow propeller drones.
A warning to go to shelters because missiles or drones may be incoming.
A fast rocket that arcs high then falls on a target. Different from a cruise missile or drone.
When air defenses destroy an incoming drone or missile before it hits.
